title: World Leader At 31: How Sebastian Kurz Became Austria’s Chancellor | FO554 Raj Shamani
text: How did you become the youngest prime minister in the world? >> My first reaction was very negative. I'm 24. I'm still at university. It's not going to work out. Media is going to kill me. >> Were you ever scared to go against someone who's the most powerful person in Europe and you're a small minister in a small country? >> We were absolutely scared. For everyone who doesn't know you and who's watching you for the first time, okay? Tell us how did you become the youngest Prime Minister in the world? I don't know anyone who's who's been 30 and has like who's become a Prime Minister at the age of 30? Like how how did that happen? >> First of all, one second, um it was not planned, to be honest. Um and it was a long uh journey. I would I I started uh in in politics more than 10 years before that. So, um to be honest, it was not planned at all. I was uh at the age of uh 16, 17, like everybody else, going to school, enjoying going out. I played tennis, but I was also interested in in politics. So, at the age of uh 17, I I started to volunteer in the youth organization of the Conservative Party in Austria. >> [snorts] >> I enjoyed it. I went there for like events twice a month or three times a month. And after a few years, then became the head of the youth organization. And I would say this was the the starting point. I I still didn't want to become a professional politician. But things went very well. The youth organization became bigger and bigger, became more and more powerful. In the end, we nearly had 100,000 members, which is a lot for small country like Austria with 9 million people. And when there was a change in the government, my party leader in these days invited me to become state secretary for integration, which is something like deputy minister. >> Just out of nowhere, he told you because you were leading the youth party. He did the party leader just asked you to become state secretary. >> Well, the youth organization was very sizable, yeah, and it was very successful. So, it was a like a powerful group within the party. So, I think it was not such a big surprise, yeah, on one hand because I was was 24. And so, when he asked me to join the government, like my my first reaction was very negative. I told him, "Look, I'm I'm 24. I'm still at university. I'm by far too young. It's not going to work out. Media is going to kill me. It's It's a bad idea." And he was patient with me and very friendly and said, "Look, you don't have to decide immediately. Take your time. Relax. Sit down for a few hours. Consult with a few people. And in a few hours, we talk again and you tell me how you decide. So, I sat down thought about it again, had the same feeling, it's impossible, it's not going to work, media is going to kill me. But after 10 minutes he came back and he looked at me and said, "Look, >> [gasps] >> I feel a bit sorry for you because I told you take your time, you have a few hours. The truth is if you discuss something in politics with a few people, people cannot keep secrets. I have to inform you it's all over the news now that you are going to be state secretary for integration, so there is no way back." So, I ended up at the age of 24 as a member of government without saying yes, without accepting the job, but a few days later I was in this position and unfortunately I was right. The start was extremely tough, media was very negative, public opinion was very negative, and I probably had the had the toughest year of my life. >> And what was the worst line you read about yourself in the media when you became almost like a deputy prime minister at the age of 24? >> Deputy minister, like I I don't remember like a single line because there were so many and all of them or nearly all of them were very negative. And and that is why it was so difficult, yeah? So, the first year in this position was really tough and [snorts] it was extremely challenging. Um and uh yeah, tried tried to perform and to convince people with our performance day by day. >> But were you the first one who became at the age of 24 became the minister as well in Austria? >> Yeah. >> So, did you ask the party chief ever like why you? Why at the age of 24 you? >> Well, I knew it was because of my position as of as the head of the youth organization. Um so, this fact was not a a big surprise. It was just like the young age that was challenging. >> So, Here's what I'm trying to understand. Like the party chief appointed you because he wanted the influence of those 100,000 people who were supporting you. Or did he see that did he see a future uh did he see a future politician in you and he wanted to recruit young more and more young people to join party? >> So, he was probably more optimistic than I was. Uh but uh unfortunately, I was right on that and he was was wrong. So, it was really a tough year. Um I think what he wanted to do and um I think this is is like what politics should look like. I think he wanted to build a very diverse team. Yeah, he wanted to have men and women, people from the city and from the countryside, older people, uh also a young guy like me. So, I think this was his idea and in in general, yeah, I think such an idea is good. It was just tough for me that I was the young guy and that I was the target. >> And then you became in next 4 years, you ended up becoming the foreign minister. How did that happen? >> Well, as I told you the first year was was super tough. The only thing that we were able to do was to work hard and thanks God things got better step by step. But I I will never forget that the a good friend of mine called me in these days and when I asked him for for advice, he said, "No, look, you don't have a lot of uh choices. I think the best thing what you can do in politics is you should try to do what you believe in, yeah. And if there's a lot of criticism, yeah, try not to focus on it, focus on your job, do your work. And if there's a lot of applause, try not to focus on it, just focus on your work and do your job. I think that's the that's the best advice I got and and that's how I tried to do my job. >> Favorite, was Is a turning point which made a young 20-year-old something become the foreign minister? Well, because everyone else in the ministry was probably twice your age. >> Absolutely. So, I I think as I told you, the beginning was super tough. We tried to do our best and we were responsible for integration of um foreigners in our country. I think what we did well is that we tried to um change the whole debate. So, what we said is you should not judge people by their origin or their religion, um but by their performance, yeah? So, we we said like focus on performance. Everybody who is in our country, no matter where he comes from, um should contribute, should work hard, should learn the language, and should be um like somebody who contributes in our society. And this approach was I think the right one, yeah? Because uh it it was not the left approach that like all foreigners are victims and they should get a lot of uh uh social uh support and and public money. And it was not a a far-right racist approach. Uh so, I think it made a lot of sense and and with this approach, I think my team and I maybe just did a good job in in in our field and it was seen very positively by a growing number of people. And this was the main reason, I think, why we got a lot of uh support in in the elections. And after that, uh I ended up in a new position. >> So, when you were the sec- uh the state secretary, at that time you introduced this immigration policy. >> Yes. >> And then that's why you ended up >> Yeah. >> What was this entire immigration policy? Because the Europe generally is seen very receptive of immigrants, right? Especially Germany, they're very loud about it. You are very close with Germany, right? You speak the same language. And yet you were blocking the migration and being like, "If somebody's just coming to your country, they should not be welcomed if they're not contributing to the society." >> Right? >> Absolutely. It's twofold. >> Absolutely. So >> How did you stand for? Because comparatively to Germany, your country is very very small. And you're a young person. >> Absolutely. Look, in 2015, the migration crisis hit Europe, especially Germany, Austria, Sweden, and a few other countries. And [snorts] um I think the main problem in these days was that the German Chancellor, Angela Merkel, had the policy of open borders and welcoming everybody who wanted to move to Germany. And I think the main problem with this policy was that so many people felt invited, yeah, that millions started to leave their home countries in order to end up in Germany, Austria, Sweden, or other Western European countries. And I think because of my experience in the work in integration, I always had the feeling that this is not going to end well. So from the beginning, I always had a different approach. We always were against the policy of open borders. We always said that um illegal migration or massive migration is extremely problematic for Europe. and we also said that integration can only work successfully if there's a limited amount of people that you have to integrate in your society. So I was always on the other side which was extremely tough because Merkel was very powerful in these days. She had a lot of public support for her position. All the media was supportive and most of the other European countries. So it was really tough, yeah, [snorts] in the year 2015 to have a different approach. Like they they said that our approach is racist and like they compared us with Hitler and the dark days. Uh uh in the dark times. Uh in our continent. So it was really really tough. Um and in these days there was no room for a rational debate, yeah? Whenever we came with these arguments, there was no rational debate. It was just emotions. And so it was it was very tough in these days. It was a small group that we formed supported by some Eastern European countries which had a very similar view, but the the big majority in in Europe was on the different side. Since then, I I would say that most people have changed their mind. Public opinion has changed, but also most of of the prime ministers today have a different view and I think that it's now, thanks God, common sense that Europe has to protect its external borders.
